## [2026-09-03] Individual Meritocratic Belief: hard-work item missing from 1999 — H1/H3 restricted to 2009/2019
**Context:** The Methodology Outline state the hard-work item (MAIN Individual Meritocratic Belief measure) is "available and coded consistently in all three waves" (1999/2009/2019).
The codebook shows this is false: the item (`v6` in the cumulation) is
explicitly marked "Variable not available in this module" for ISSP 1999 —
it only exists in 1987, 1992, 2009, and 2019. Cross-checked directly against
the 1999 questionnaire PDF (`ZA3430_bq.pdf`): the 1999 "getting ahead"
battery asked about wealthy family and knowing the right people only, not
hard work. Same problem, worse, for the ambition item (`v4`, the two-item
robustness measure's second component): available only in 1987/1992/2009 —
missing from BOTH 1999 and 2019, not just 2019 as previously assumed.
**Decision:** H1 and H3 (both use `ind_belief_c` as a moderator) are
restricted to the 2009 and 2019 waves only. 1999 is dropped from these two
models explicitly, not left in and relying on implicit listwise deletion — the 
sample restriction should be stated plainly in the methods/results write-up, not
buried. The two-item robustness check (hard work + ambition) is now a 
single-wave (2009-only) check, not a 1999/2009 comparison — `wave` was dropped 
from that model's formula since it would otherwise be a constant with no 
variation.
**Why this matters:** this shrinks the effective sample for the chapter's
two central, novel hypotheses (H1, H3) by a full wave and needs a
limitations-section footnote.

## [2026-10-26] Building from scratch: recodes verified against codebook labels
**Context:** Building the pipeline in a new repo (`CH1_recognition_injury`).
**Decision:** Every code (`sss`, `credential`, `ind_belief`, `income`, `gender`, 
`age`) was checked against the value labels and with old-vs-new cross-tabs 
before use. Negative codes (-9/-8/-7/-3/-1) → `NA`. `ind_belief` = 6 − `v6` (5 = 
strongest hard-work endorsement). Stratification direction checked
(Austria/Germany/Hungary = 8; Australia/Canada/NZ/USA = 0).

## [2026-10-27] ISEI missing for ~19.5% of respondents
**What I found:** Almost all are ISCO-88 missing codes (mainly -4: respondents 
with no job), not lookup gaps; code 110 (armed forces, 482 cases) is the only 
real unmatched code.
**Decision:** Left as `NA`. Non-working respondents drop out of any model with 
occupational status; this goes in the attrition table.

## [2026-10-27] Tertiary enrolment (WDI) missing for six sample country-waves
**What I found:** Australia, Germany, Japan, New Zealand, Portugal and the USA 
have no `SE.TER.ENRR` value for 2006–2012 in the download, so none for the 2009 
wave. This is why the old main model had 25 countries (Portugal drops out 
entirely; Canada has only 1999).
**Decision:** Baseline keeps `tertiary` as `NA` (no interpolation). Five 
countries enter the main model with 2019 only. Planned sensitivity check: refit 
without `tertiary` as a control.

## [2026-10-27] Respondents aged 15–17 kept
**Decision:** Only `AGE = -9` set to `NA`. 455 respondents aged 15–17 and one 
aged 105 are retained. Restricting to 18+ is a possible sensitivity check.
  
## [2026-10-27] Analytic sample 
**Decision:** Sample built by sequential filters, recording n and countries after each step:
118,200 (35 countries) → waves 2009 + 2019: 87,019 (34) → has a stratification 
value: 60,945 (26) → complete on all model variables: 38,010 (25). 
Same as the old pipeline (25 countries,n = 38,010). `drop_na()` names the model 
variables explicitly. Canada leaves at the wave step (1999 only); the 8 
countries without OECD coverage leave at the stratification step; Portugal
leaves at the complete-case step (no 2019 wave, tertiary missing in 2009).

## [2026-10-27] Missingness is patterned by country and not by wave
**Result (26-country sample, before complete cases):** income missing 17.8% 
(largest loss), 7% (Norway) to 43% (Portugal); ISEI 12.7% (Spain 32%, Japan 31%); 
tertiary 12.7%. By wave: income 17.8% vs 17.9%; ISEI 14.6% (2009) vs 10.6% (2019). 
Income missingness is respondent non-response (-9/-8/-7), not an unasked item 
(no -1 codes in the high-missing countries). Individually lost respondents: 
income 10,857; ISEI 7,768; tertiary 7,732; sss 1,202; ind_belief 906; 
credential 672; age 408; gender 126 (overlap explains why they sum to more than 
the 22,935 lost).

## [2026-10-27] Retention by country is uneven
**Result:** complete-case retention ranges from 0% (Portugal) to 84% (Sweden). 
Australia keeps 658 respondents, Spain 486, Switzerland 3,077. Australia, 
Germany, Japan, USA and New Zealand contribute 2019 only (tertiary gap). The low 
end of stratification (Australia, NZ, USA) is hit hardest.

## [2026-10-27] Sensitivity sample without tertiary
**Result:** dropping `tertiary` from the complete-case rule gives n = 43,211 in 
26 countries (Portugal returns; five countries regain their 2009 wave). Planned 
as a robustness run.

## [2026-10-27] The analytic sample is selected
**Result:** sample at each step (2009/2019 data → 26 countries → complete cases): 
mean SSS 5.20 → 5.41 → 5.46; tertiary share 25.6% → 27.3% → 30.7%; 
mean age 48.4 → 50.2 → 50.9. The SSS rise comes from the country filter 
(the 8 dropped countries average SSS 4.70); the tertiary rise comes from the 
complete-case step.

## [2026-10-27] Univariate descriptives (n = 38,010)
**Result:** SSS mean 5.46, SD 1.72, range 1–10, roughly bell-shaped (histogram, binwidth 1).
Belief (1–5): mean 3.89, SD 0.90, median 4, upper quartile at the maximum (ceiling); 
+1 SD is about 0.9 of a scale point. ISEI mean 46.4 (SD 17.5, 16–90); 
age mean 50.9 (SD 16.3, 15–99). 30.7% tertiary; income terciles 32/33/35%; 
52.7% female; 45% 2009, 55% 2019.

**Plots:** SSS roughly bell-shaped; income terciles nearly even (top tercile slightly
over-represented); belief strongly left-skewed with mode at 4 (about 70% in categories 4–5,
only about 6% in 1–2); ISEI multimodal (clusters near 30, 50 and 70) because it takes
discrete values by occupation group. Limitation noted: few low-belief respondents.

## [2026-10-28] Pipeline cleanup: sample and descriptives in one script, outputs organized
**Decision:** `03_descriptive.R` builds the analytic sample (all rows → waves 2009 + 2019 →
stratification present → complete on `model_vars`, defined once) and runs the descriptives.

## [2026-10-28] Distribution plots
**Result:** SSS roughly bell-shaped (peak at 5–6). Income terciles nearly even. Belief strongly
left-skewed: mode at 4, about 70% in categories 4–5, about 6% in 1–2 (few low-belief
respondents). ISEI multimodal (clusters near 30, 50, 70) because it takes discrete values by
occupation group.

## [2026-10-28] Group descriptives
**Result:** Raw credential gap = 1.14 SSS points (6.25 vs 5.11). Gap by belief level (1–5):
1.04, 0.88, 1.10, 1.14, 1.16; no clear fan-out in the raw means; both groups flatten between
belief 4 and 5; the tertiary belief-1 cell has only 96 respondents. Correlations: credential–ISEI
0.51 (largest), SSS–credential 0.30, SSS–ISEI 0.35, SSS–belief 0.07, belief–credential 0.04.
**Decision:** 1.14 is the benchmark for the model's credential coefficient. Check
credential–ISEI collinearity in the diagnostics.

## [2026-10-28] Country-level descriptives
**Result:** 25 countries, 40 country-waves: 15 with both waves, 5 with 2009 only, 5 with 2019
only. Stratification has 7 distinct values; Italy (4), Switzerland (6) and the Czech Republic (7)
are alone at their value. Country mean SSS 3.96 (Hungary) to 6.46 (New Zealand); tertiary
share 5% to 58%. Country-level correlations: stratification–tertiary share −0.47,
tertiary share–mean SSS +0.77. WDI tertiary enrolment is a gross ratio (110 in Australia 2019).

## [2026-10-28] Tertiary cut (DEGREE = 5) is not equally clean across countries
**Result:** DEGREE category 4 is 20–34% of respondents in Switzerland, Denmark, Australia,
Lithuania, Germany, Finland, New Zealand and Japan, about as large as category 5 in several.
Hungary: 18.0% in category 4 vs 4.75% in category 5 (its 5% tertiary share is probably a
coding artifact). Small in the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Austria and Sweden.
**Decision:** Keep DEGREE = 5 as the main measure.

## [2026-10-28] `credential_alt` built (DEGREE >= 4) for robustness
**Result:** Categories 0–3 → 0 (74,353), 4–5 → 1 (42,609), -9 → NA (1,238), the same missing
values as the main `credential`, so the analytic sample is unchanged (n = 38,010, 25 countries).
**Decision:** Main model keeps `credential` (DEGREE = 5); `credential_alt` is used only in the
robustness run.


## [2026-10-28] Credential share by country and wave
**Result:** Among the 15 two-wave countries, tertiary share (DEGREE = 5) rises 2009 → 2019 by
+52 (Denmark), +28 (France), +25 (Switzerland), +23 (Sweden), +22 (Norway), +21 (Israel),
+20 (Iceland) and +15 (Finland) points; it is stable (|change| < 7) in Austria, Chile, Czech
Republic, Great Britain, Italy, Lithuania and Slovenia. Mean +14.7. Single-wave countries:
2009-only share 5–20% (Hungary, Slovakia, Poland, Spain, Latvia); 2019-only 26–58%
(Japan, Germany, USA, NZ, Australia). The country-level stratification–tertiary correlation
(-0.47) is partly a coding artifact (Australia, NZ, USA are 2019-only).

## [2026-10-28] Supervisor reply: harmonize education across waves
**Anthony:** unbalanced country-wave structure must be accounted for in the nesting and limits the
conclusions, but is not particularly problematic. Recommends making the education variable as
similar as possible across waves: recode from the national degree variables (may need the
separate wave files) or consider EDUCYRS (possibly non-linear; ideally with published precedent).
**Check:** the cumulation DEGREE boundary between 4 and 5 differs by country and wave (2019 cat 5
= first-stage tertiary, cat 6 = Master/Doctor; 2009 boundary varies). EDUCYRS has outlier codes
and needs cleaning; where clean it is stable across waves while DEGREE = 5 jumps 20–28 points.
Israel's jump is not explained by coding.
**Decision (pending):** build a country-by-wave crosswalk from national degree variables.

## 2026-10-28 Harmonizing the tertiary credential across ISSP 2009 and 2019

**Context**
The DEGREE variable changes meaning between waves: 2009 categories are derived
from national degree variables, and 2019 follows ISCED-97. DEGREE = 5 therefore 
means different things in the two waves, and the tertiary share jumped for 
countries observed in both (for example Italy 4% to 25%). Anthony advised 
recoding from the national-level degree variables (XX_DEGR).

**What went wrong**
Using DEGREE = 5 as the credential made the change in credential prevalence 
between waves partly a coding artifact. This was confounded with country because 
10 countries appear in only one wave.

**Decision**
I built a country-by-wave crosswalk (data/codebooks/degree_crosswalk.csv, 504 rows) 
from the national degree categories and coded harmonized_tertiary by label, not by DEGREE.
Rule: 1 = completed degree at bachelor level or higher (bachelor, master, doctorate, long university degrees, and bachelor-level degrees from universities of applied sciences or polytechnics, about three or more years). 0 = everything else, including incomplete university, short-cycle or technical tertiary under 3 years, higher vocational, Meister and apprenticeships, post-secondary non-tertiary, and school levels.
Ambiguous categories were decided by the rule, with median years of education as a tie-breaker only. 
Kept as 0 and flagged: Chile non-university higher education and Swiss higher vocational training (ISCED 6 in some classifications). Kept as 1 and flagged: Swiss "Uni diploma (intermediary level)" and "Bachelor + short degree", and Swedish 2009 "University degree" (may include short degrees).

**Result**
The crosswalk is complete with no duplicate keys. 


## 2026-10-28 Harmonized tertiary credential from national degree variables
**Context**
DEGREE changes meaning between 2009 and 2019, and Anthony advised recoding from the national degree variables.
**What went wrong**
First join key (v2) was the data version string, not an ID; the iso code was built after country was overwritten inside transmute, giving 100% missing credential. My first check passed vacuously.
**Decision**
Built a country-by-wave crosswalk (504 rows) and coded credential = completed bachelor-level or higher degree, decided by category label. ID is v3 (2009) and caseid (2019), validated against the cumulation (53,213 rows, tertiary split agrees). Old DEGREE = 5 kept as credential_degree5.
**Result**
Wave-to-wave jumps shrink (Denmark +50 to +13 points) but real rises remain (Israel, Czech Republic). Sample unchanged (n = 38,010, 25 countries). Crosswalk omits 2009 for AU, DE, JP, NZ, US.
**Status**
Done for the main sample. Open: extend crosswalk, ISCO-88 robustness variant, centering decision.

## 2026-10-30 EDUCYRS as an alternative to DEGREE 
**Context**
Anthony suggested EDUCYRS, perhaps cubed, ideally with published precedent. Built in a separate script (05_educyrs_variant.R) so the main pipeline is untouched.
**What went wrong**
I found no published precedent for cubing years of schooling. EDUCYRS has its own wave discontinuity: it rises between waves in most countries, and Switzerland jumps 3.3 years (11.4 to 14.7) because the 2009 answers cluster at 9 years. It is also missing for 94.5% of rows only (versus 98.9% for DEGREE), unevenly by country. My earlier note that its means were stable across waves was wrong for Switzerland, France and Israel.
**Decision**
Keep the crosswalk credential as the main measure. Use EDUCYRS (raw and cubed) only as a sensitivity analysis, and ask Anthony for the paper he had in mind.
**Result**
Cubed years correlate .89 with raw years and .62 with tertiary (.60 raw), but change the construct from lacking a credential to graded schooling.
**Status**
Done for now. Open: run the EDUCYRS sensitivity models after the main models.
